extracted.intended_audience: students of political philosophy, legislators, and readers of classical political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Aristotle's practical criteria for constituting a well-ordered city/state: what offices, population size, territory, civic character, economic arrangements, and institutions are necessary for a city to exist and enable citizens to live a happy/virtuous life. Intended to guide legislators and political thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary magistrates and departmental organization
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be civil magistrates for distinct departments (religion, war, taxes, expenditures, markets, public buildings, harbours, highways) and other officers to carry on the public business of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle enumerates a nearly complete set of public offices: magistrates for military command, finance, public works, markets, and religious care. He notes that in very small cities several duties may be combined in one person, while in larger states offices are divided and sometimes form councils. Example usages: separate commanders for cavalry, light-armed troops, bowmen, and sailors; preadvisers or councils to preside. Anti-pattern: leaving important departments unmanaged or lumping incompatible functions together without oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military organization and command hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a state has different forces (horse, light-armed, bowmen, sailors) it should put distinct commanders over each division with subordinate officers, forming a joined military body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle stresses clear chains of command and specialised military offices so the whole force composes one effective military body. Guidance implies specialization according to arms and explicit delegation of authority. Anti-patterns include ill-defined commands or mixing incompatible military roles under a single, unskilled commander.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal oversight and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Because some magistrates handle public money, it is necessary to have officers whose sole employment is to take account of public funds and correct mismanagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal officers must exist to audit, account for revenues and taxes, and correct mismanagement. This ensures responsible disposal of public revenue and prevents corruption. Example: one magistrate often has disposal of public revenue but must be balanced by officers who account for what they have. Anti-pattern: concentrating revenue control with no accounting officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme magistrate / presiding officer
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be one magistrate supreme over others who can summon and preside over the people and often has disposal of public revenue and taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This officer provides unity of public procedure — calling assemblies, presiding as head of state. Aristotle notes different names (preadvisers, councils) and that the form (single or many) varies by constitution. Guidance: ensure legitimacy and clear constitutional role for whoever presides. Anti-pattern: absence of any authorized presiding officer or unclear supremacy leading to disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious establishment and sacred officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons must be assigned to religion: priests, keepers/builders of temples, officers of sacred revenue, and persons to take general care of public sacrifices not entrusted to priests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion and public worship are essential public charges. Duties can be vested in one or many depending on city size; some religious functions distinct from priesthood (e.g., temple maintenance, sacred-revenue officers). Guidance: maintain temples, repair or rebuild when necessary; ensure sacred rites are conducted. Anti-pattern: neglecting religious offices or leaving sacred revenue uncontrolled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial infrastructure and law-enforcement offices
rubrics_metrics.description: A city requires courts to determine causes, scribes to enrol private contracts, guards over prisoners, officers to execute laws, councils on either side, and officers to watch the conduct of judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functioning justice system is essential: recording contracts, secure detention, enforcing law, and oversight of magistrates and judges. Aristotle emphasizes courts as 'first of all in necessity' for civil society. Anti-patterns include weak record-keeping, no oversight of judges, or absence of enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized magistracies for social functions and public life
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular magistrates may be appointed for non-universal but useful functions: governance of women, supervision of boys' education, care of gymnastic exercises, theatres, and public spectacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In states with leisure and attention to order, assign officers for education, public entertainments, and social governance. Some roles are not generally useful (e.g., governors of women) where social circumstances (lack of slaves) make household labour necessary. Guidance: appoint specialists only where they serve the common good and are practicable. Anti-pattern: creating offices purely ceremonial or that undermine virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: City size: optimal population and manageable numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The city's population should be sufficient for self-defence and to enable inhabitants to live happily in political community, yet not so large that magistrates cannot know the characters of fellow-citizens or govern effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greatness should be judged by strength to accomplish the state's ends rather than raw numbers. There is a determinate size: too small lacks defence capacity; too large becomes a nation (not a city) and is hard to govern (risk of strangers, sojourners assuming citizen rights). Guidance: choose a population large enough for self-sufficiency and defence but limited so magistrates can exercise informed governance. Anti-pattern: indiscriminate enlargement of citizen body or confusing population size with greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of greatness by capability/power rather than headcount
rubrics_metrics.description: A state's greatness is the power it has to accomplish its objectives (e.g., defence), not merely the multitude of inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle gives the example: a physician's greatness is not bodily size but skill. Similarly, value the composition (soldiers vs mechanics) and the ability to perform the state's ends. Anti-pattern: equating numeric population with political strength or neglecting composition of citizenry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial quality and defensible situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Country/territory should supply necessaries of life, be of extent enabling ease and freedom for inhabitants, be difficult of access to enemies but easy to inhabitants, and be situated to assist and receive supplies (ideally near sea but with defensive considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess soil productive capacity, size appropriate to living at ease, and strategic position. For position ask military-skills advisors. Guidance: territory must enable defense and supply; where possible maritime access helps but must be regulated. Anti-patterns: placing city in indefensible location or with insufficient resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime power and controlled commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Maritime (sea) access is advantageous for defence, supply, and appearance of strength; a naval force is necessary to a degree. But a resort of persons with different habits (merchants) may be disserviceable by impeding laws and multiplying citizens to govern; the city should traffic to supply its own wants, not to serve others, and regulate who may have intercourse with the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage naval capacity proportionate to the state's vigour; regulate maritime commerce so it serves local needs rather than unbounded profit-seeking. Where docks/harbours exist, isolate them from citadel and legally define permitted intercourse. Anti-pattern: unrestricted commercial openness that undermines civic virtue or allows alien influences to dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural disposition of citizens: courage blended with intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens should be both sensible (quick in understanding/arts) and courageous; different climates/nations foster different traits, but the best citizens blend both, enabling freedom and good governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses ethnographic examples (northerners courageous but lacking arts, Asiatics quick in arts but deficient in courage, Greeks balanced). Guidance: cultivate and select citizens with both courage and practical judgment to obey a legislator who makes laws aiming at virtue. Anti-pattern: a citizen body skewed to one extreme (courage without skill, or skill without courage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of government: enable virtuous activity leading to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The best government is that which is so established that every one may have it in their power to act virtuously and live happily; happiness consists in virtuous activity and the city that acts best is happiest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation and constitution should be judged by their capacity to foster virtue and wise action among citizens. Debate exists whether contemplative or political active life is superior; Aristotle argues the active life in the city is central because virtuous activity produces noble ends. Anti-pattern: constitutions promoting wealth/power at expense of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of occupations: exclude mechanics and trade from citizen rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In the best-governed states citizens (those entitled to rights) should not exercise mechanic employment or commerce, which are ignoble and destructive to virtue; husbandry should be performed by others (slaves, servants) to leave citizens leisure for virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle insists citizens must be free from ignoble labour to pursue political and virtuous life; landed property should belong to them to secure their status. Guidance: separate productive labour from political rights; anti-pattern: allowing mechanical trades and mercantile preoccupations to dominate the citizen class, thus undermining virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of public offices by natural ability and age
rubrics_metrics.description: Different employments require different abilities; where courage and judgment differ by age, allot what requires courage to the young and what requires judgment to the old; where feasible, the same person may perform multiple roles if they possess required qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign roles (soldier, senator, judge) according to natural aptitudes and life-stage: courage tends to youth, wisdom to age. But where necessary (those with arms) positions may be concentrated due to political realities. Anti-pattern: rigid, age-blind assignment or forcing ill-suited persons into offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential components without which a city cannot exist
rubrics_metrics.description: A city must be capable of procuring: (1) food, (2) arts (crafts and instruments), (3) arms (armed force), (4) revenue (for internal needs and war), (5) a religious establishment, and (6) a court to determine criminal and civil causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames these six as absolutely necessary. Legislators should ensure institutional provision of these necessities (farmers, artificers, soldiers, rich men, priests, judges). Anti-pattern: neglecting any of these fundamentals (e.g., no armed defence, no revenue, no courts) which makes cityhood impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: necessary but distinct from the state; community as equals' purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Property is necessary but is not itself the state; a city is a community of equals aiming at the best life; differences in opportunity (some great, some little) cause different modes of living and governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize private property's role without conflating it with political community; design institutions to enable equality in participation in the virtuous life where appropriate. Anti-pattern: treating property relations as the essence of the polity rather than instruments for citizens' good.
